newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Sluggish British manufacturing poses dilemma.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sluggish British manufacturing poses dilemma.

text.p: British manufacturing output grew slightly in February, official data showed on Wednesday, but it still badly lagged the service sector, highlighting a dilemma for the new government after the May 1 general election.

The Office of National Statistics (ONS) said manufacturing output grew 0.2 percent in February for year-on-year growth of 1.8 percent. The wider measure of industrial production, which includes utilities output, fell by 0.6 percent in February.

Despite the small pick up in manufacturing, growth in the export-dependent sector is very sluggish compared with the rocketing service industries which has been the main beneficiary so far of robust domestic consumer demand.

Economists said this suggested an imbalance in the economy and presented a dilemma for the incoming chancellor of the exchequer (finance minister) in gauging the correct mix of monetary and fiscal policy.
"The output figures do confirm some imbalance of growth," said UBS economist Alex Garrard.

"They weigh against an interest rate hike in the sense that they show only a little pick up in manufacturing activity, but clearly highlight the dilemma for an incoming chancellor who needs to do something to establish anti-inflationary credentials."
The next chancellor is widely expected to be opposition economics spokesman Gordon Brown as the Labour party is far ahead in opinion polls.
If he raised interest rates to fend off inflationary pressures, he would run the risk of an even stronger pound and further weakness in the manufacturing sector.

The pound has rallied steadily over the last eight months -- gaining around 17 percent on a trade-weighted basis -- fuelling fears that the high exchange rate is hitting exports by pushing up prices for overseas buyers.
Analysts said the worst was yet to come in terms of sterling's dampening effect on exports, and would be more strongly felt in the summer.
"But stronger sterling and an interest rate rise could halt the moderate recovery dead in its tracks," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Securities.
In the meantime domestic demand is providing a much-needed prop to the manufacturing industry.
A strong 2.7 percent rise in the output of durable goods in the three months to February in particular suggests that domestic demand is helping to offset the effect of sterling.

No analyst polled by Reuters expected an increase to be announced at Thursday's monthly meeting between the Bank of England Governor Eddie George and present conservative Chancellor Kenneth Clarke. But rates are forecast to rise after the election regardless of the outcome.
Prime Minister John Major underlined those expectations on Wednesday when he said he "would not hestitate to act to keep inflation under control".

But a better policy mix for strong domestic demand, a strong currency and a weak manufacturing sector would be to leave base rates at 6.0 percent and rely on tighter fiscal policy to curb growth instead, many economists now say.
With both main parties committed to no income tax rises after the election, the scope for fiscal tightening is limited to higher indirect taxes.
Garrard said the most likely advice from Brown's Treasury team would be to tighten fiscal policy eventually, but put up base rates in the short term.

The economy was showing signs of imbalance when Clarke took a penny off income tax in his budget in November last year. This would give Brown someone to blame for any unpopular tax rises if he chose to bite the bullet, Garrard said.

"If we do get a new administration we get another chance to tighten fiscal policy and it gives Gordon Brown the opportunity to blame policy moves on mistakes made by the previous government," he said.
